items.title: US business activity growth eases further in November, survey shows By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 23 (Reuters) - US business activity growth slowed further in November as high prices held back new orders and capacity constraints restrained output, but overall activity remains resilient, suggesting economic growth is continuing at an above-trend rate, a survey showed on Monday. S&P Global said its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, tracking the manufacturing and services sectors, eased to a four-month low of 54.6 this month from a final reading of 55.9 in October. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. The pace of growth slackened in both manufacturing and the vast services sector, which is responsible for roughly two-thirds of US economic activity. The manufacturing PMI slipped to a three-month low of 54.5 from 54.9 in October, while the services PMI dropped to a four-month low of 54.7 from 56.1 last month. New business in services slid, while new orders in manufacturing were little changed. Input cost pressures eased but remain elevated and suggest inflation overall will stay well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target. "Although output growth slowed in November, recent readings have been impressively strong, and the PMI surveys still point to GDP (gross domestic product) rising at an annualized rate of about 3% in the fourth quarter," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Growth also remained encouragingly broad-based across both manufacturing and services, with both sectors also still taking on additional staff in numbers that are indicative of a further strong payroll gain during November." The US economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate in the third quarter thanks to ongoing strength in consumer spending and the frenetic artificial intelligence build-out, and employers added a greater-than-expected 165,000 workers to their payrolls in October. "A key concern is the elevated cost of living and resulting pressures on affordability, and the survey price gauges remain at levels consistent with inflation running well above the Fed’s 2% target in the coming months, despite some moderation of the rate of inflation in November," Williamson said. "Supply disruptions, widely linked to global shipping delays, also appear to have become more widespread, adding to firms’ concerns about being able to fulfill orders and likely to add further to underlying price pressures in the coming months." The November 12-20 survey period also dovetailed with a sharp selloff in the US stock market, which has been a key pillar supporting consumer spending, on concerns about the sustainability of the AI boom. It was not clear from the survey data whether that development contributed to the softening in this month’s PMI readings.

items.title: What could Democrats do with their expanding congressional majority? | Politics News | Al Jazeera
items.excerpt: The Democratic Party has continued to expand its already sizeable majorities in the United States Congress as counting concludes in the final races of the 2026 midterm elections. As of Monday, the Democrats hold a 258-seat majority in the 435-member House of Representatives. Four races remain uncalled. All the races have been decided, meanwhile, for the Senate, where Democrats gained a 56-seat majority out of 100 total seats. Flipping both chambers gives the party a strong hand to shape legislation during the last two years of Trump’s term in office. How might the Democrats approach their role in government once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3? ... ## What do the results say? The midterm results give Democrats their largest House majority since 1992 and their largest Senate majority in more than a decade. Republicans, meanwhile, saw their tally in the House drop to 173 seats, their lowest figure in years. The vote also served as a firm rebuke of Trump’s second term as president, with voters venting their frustration over cost-of-living issues, the US-Israel war on Iran, aggressive immigration raids and corruption. Democratic victories also extended well beyond traditional left-wing strongholds, with candidates racking up wins in Republican-led states such as Texas, Mississippi and South Carolina. ... ## What will Democrats do with their majority? Democrats have long pledged to use any congressional majorities they win as a check on Trump’s agenda. But the scale of their success in the 2026 midterms has prompted discussion about embracing a more ambitious legislative agenda. In the House of Representatives, Democrats have outlined a 100-day agenda that includes potentially reversing tax cuts that largely benefit wealthy earners and restoring healthcare subsidies that expired under Trump. Lawmakers have also said that they will act to end the war on Iran, although divisions remain within the party over how to rein in Trump’s military actions. Under the US Constitution, Congress alone can authorise military operations. Progressives have accused the party’s moderate wing of playing down expectations of firm steps to end the war, including cutting off funding. Democrats have also pledged to use their newfound position to exercise oversight over the executive branch by launching probes and issuing subpoenas. On Monday, for example, House Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said that a Democrat-led Congress would conduct a “swift, thorough, and wide-ranging” investigation into the actions of the chip manufacturer Nvidia. He also said it would delve into the “corrupt abuse of power” by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. In the Senate, Democrats have also threatened to block Trump’s nominees for high-level government positions, which require the chamber’s confirmation. ... While Democrats will hold substantial majorities in both chambers of Congress, Trump will retain the power to veto legislation.

One week after attending the Los Angeles premiere of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth in Los Angeles, the actor unexpectedly skipped the Netflix movie’s red carpet rollout in London due to illness. Ahead of the Nov. 23 event, its organizers told British outlet The Independent in a statement that Pitt was “is no longer able to attend the premiere as he has come down with flu and has been advised not to travel." Amid his sickness, the 62-year-old made the decision to focus on the long-term health of himself and his cast. “He has had the flu for a few days and didn’t want to get anyone sick,” a source close to Pitt told E! News. “He is recovering and looking forward to future screenings.” Pitt’s costars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller, as well as director David Fincher, still attended the premiere, which was held at the BFI IMAX in the English capital.
